newsitem.title: USA: Melting snow triggers flooding in North Dakota.
newsitem.headline: Melting snow triggers flooding in North Dakota.

text.p: Runoff from melting snow flooded hundreds of homes across North Dakota on Sunday, as ice jams sent rivers pouring out of their banks.
Several residents had to evacuate Beulah and Hazen, North Dakota, two small towns roughly 50 miles (80 km) northwest of Bismarck where the Knife River spilled over its banks.
"People are being cut off by the snow melt drainage, in some cases by snow right around their homes," National Weather Service hydrologist Charlene Prindeville in Bismarck said.
The Weather Service issued flood warnings for broad areas of western and south central North Dakota after two consecutive days of temperatures in the 50s (10-13 Celsius) began melting the snowpack.
In some cases, areas nowhere near rivers were flooded by melting snow that formed ponds on the flat terrain. Some local roads were impassable, Prindeville said.

Tributaries of the Missouri River, which flow through the center of the state and later into the Mississippi by St. Louis, Missouri, were not able to dump their swollen contents because of ice coating the Missouri's banks.

Extensive spring flooding had been anticipated for weeks since the region endured one of its worst winters, with record snow accumulating in parts of North and South Dakota and Minnesota. Sandbagging operations have been underway, and dikes and levees reinforced.
Some of the most severe flooding was expected along the Red River in eastern North Dakota where up to nine feet (3 m) of accumulated snowpack was just beginning to melt.
The forecast for rain mixed with snow in central North Dakota could add to the miseries, with up to eight inches (20 cm) of heavy, wet snow expected to fall on Monday on the Red River Valley.
